Each row loads its byte's cursor `ftab[c]` (an indexed array, so it lives in memory) and stores `ftab[c] + 1`. # The build's windows cut into runs: registration and instruction count

Registered before any timing of this branch. The decision rule may be amended only in a commit
made before the first bench comment on this PR, and each amendment says what changed and why.

## What was tried before, and why this is not a retry

- **#169** (`2026-11-05-build-run-vectors.md`): the 16 entries of an all-equal window written
  as four SSE2 vectors. −2.4% of `decode_block`'s instructions, the build stage −3.1% at
  1 thread beyond noise, no `wikidata` figure beyond noise. Closed as not shown.
- **#23**: the build in four interleaved quarters, +11–12%. Rejected.
- **The run-fed line** (#266, #269, #277): the table filled from MTF's run records. Its census
  found that the build already stores 82% of Wikidata's rows through the 16-row path, and its
  stage run found the build "not store-bound" (R_floor 0.321, R_warm 1.010): what binds is its
  latency or its instructions, not its stores.
- **The census** (`2026-11-05-binding-census.md`, item 7) disfavours a write-combining build:
  the build's co-run excess tracks its low IPC, not its number of store streams.
- **The ISA probe** (#201): an x86-64-v3 build buys at most −4.5% of the build.

So no store-side lever (write-combining, prefetchw, two-pass bucketing) is tried here. This
change goes after a latency the earlier work did not name.

## The mechanism

`build_one_pass` takes the rows 16 at a time. A window of 16 equal bytes is one cursor step.
Any other window takes 16 one-row steps, and each step loads its byte's cursor `ftab[c]`,
writes the entry and stores `ftab[c] + 1`. `ftab` is an indexed array, so it lives in memory.
When a row's byte equals its predecessor's, that load must wait for the store just made: a
store-to-load forward, about 4–7 cycles on the runners' cores, on a chain as long as the run.

**How much of it there is (counted, `window_stats.rs`, all 473 blocks of
`wikidata-independent.bz2`, 235.8M rows):**
- 83.4% of rows are in all-equal windows (the run-fed census's 82%).
- The other 16.6% are in 2.45M mixed windows, 6.8 runs each on average, bimodal: 2–4 runs
  (windows at a run's edge, 47% of mixed windows) or 13–16 (literal stretches).
- **22.6M rows (9.6% of all rows, 58% of mixed-window rows) equal their predecessor inside a
  mixed window.** Each is one link of a store-forward chain today. At about 6 cycles a link,
  serial, that is up to about 0.58 cycles a row, against a whole build of about 1.4–2.2
  cycles a row on CI (the run-fed stage tables; the ISA probe's 2.17 c/B on the 7763).
  Out-of-order overlap with other rows hides part of it; how much is what this PR measures.

**The change.** A window's run heads come from one SSE2 compare of the window with itself
shifted by a byte (`run_heads`: bit j set where row j starts a run). Then:
- one run (the old 16-row path): one cursor step of 16 and one 16-wide write, now SSE2
  (`run16`, #169's kernel);
- at most `RUNS` = 6 runs: each run is one cursor step of its length L and one 16-wide
  write at its slot. The entries above the run's end (L..16) are garbage in slots of the same
  bucket above its new cursor, each overwritten by the step that later reaches it. A run with
  fewer than 16 slots left in its bucket (0.7% of mixed-window runs) takes one-row steps;
- more than 6 runs: the one-row steps as before. Those windows are mostly unequal neighbours,
  so their chains are short.

The safety argument changes from "every slot written exactly once" to "every slot last written
with its entry": the end check (every cursor at its bucket's end) still proves it, since every
garbage slot lies above some step's end inside its bucket, and the cursor passed it later.
Writes stay inside `[ftab[c], lim[c]) ⊆ [0, n)`. Refused counts still leave the table empty.
Other targets than x86_64 take a scalar `run_heads` and `run16` (the same table, checked by
the tests with the x86 paths compiled out, locally).

## Whole decoder: instructions

Inclusive Ir of the driver's `measured` (one `decode_block` on a fresh `Scratch`), both arms
built with the driver of `2026-11-05-deferred-flag-walk/` (rustc 1.99.1, fat LTO,
`codegen-units = 1`), on `wikidata-independent.bz2` (sha256 prefix `7f5c9a0044e5a305`).
Master is b68171223. Profiles and outputs are in `cg/` (`base-*` master, `head-*` this branch).

| block | master | this branch | change | build, master → branch | walk | output |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|
| 0 (54 B) | 7,037 | 7,117 | +80 | 3,200 → 3,280 | — | identical |
| 1 | 19,258,148 | 18,652,917 | −605,231 (−3.14%) | 5,250,956 → 4,645,725 (−11.5%) | 9,493,915 both | identical |
| 41 | 18,608,504 | 17,945,904 | −662,600 (−3.56%) | 5,103,413 → 4,440,813 (−13.0%) | 9,303,521 both | identical |
| 97 (56 B) | 7,481 | 7,561 | +80 | 3,368 → 3,448 | — | identical |
| 233 | 19,053,756 | 18,550,598 | −503,158 (−2.64%) | 5,038,522 → 4,535,364 (−10.0%) | 9,464,794 both | identical |
| 400 | 18,620,609 | 17,988,154 | −632,455 (−3.40%) | 5,026,554 → 4,394,099 (−12.6%) | 9,362,918 both | identical |
| 472 (70 B) | 8,252 | 8,357 | +105 | 3,585 → 3,690 | — | identical |

- **Build, walk, rest:** the whole difference is in the build. The walk is identical to the
  instruction; the rest (MTF, the call) is unchanged. The short blocks' +80 to +105 is the
  window loop's set-up on a block of three or four windows.
- **What the instructions are, by `RUNS` on block 1** (`cg/runs*-b1.out`): 1 (= #169's
  all-equal path only) 4,632,711; 3: 4,615,193; 4: 4,581,583; **6: 4,645,725**; 8: 4,757,576;
  16: 5,713,723. So **almost all of the instruction saving is #169's**, which CI already
  showed is invisible end to end. At `RUNS` = 6 the run-by-run path costs +13k instructions
  over `RUNS` = 1 on block 1 (+0.07% of the decode). **This PR's claim is not its
  instruction count.** It is the chain it removes.
- **Branches** (callgrind's simulated predictor, block 1, `cg/br-*-b1.out`): the build's
  conditional branches 564k → 376k, its simulated mispredictions 10.5k → 15.5k (+5.0k). At
  about 15 cycles each that is about +75k cycles, against about 86k chain links removed on
  the block (9.6% of 900k rows) at 4–7 cycles each, about 350–600k cycles if they were
  serial. The simulator is not the runners' predictor.

## The prediction and its falsifier

- **The build stage** (`phases`, 1 thread): **−7% to −20%**. Its instructions fall 10–13%,
  but #169's same instruction saving alone moved the stage −3.1%, so the chain must supply the
  rest.
- **`wikidata`:** 1 thread −1% to −3% wall; 4 threads −1% to −4% (the build's co-run
  inflation, ×1.4–2.3, should make a latency cut count more there, per the census's item 7).
- **No other stage moves.**
- **Falsifier:** if the build stage gains no more than #169's −3.1% (its point estimate at or
  above −4%), the store-forward chain is not what costs the build, and the mechanism is
  refuted, whatever the end-to-end figures say. A build stage that is slower refutes it too.

## The decision rule

- **Correctness (required):** CI green, Miri included (`miri_build_one_pass` reaches the
  run-by-run path, the near-end fallback and refused counts); the same bytes on every corpus
  in every bench run; the build's tests pass, with their inputs now including runs of 3–7.
- **Benefit (required):** on `wikidata` at 1 or 4 threads, the CPU change or the wall change
  excludes zero on the faster side in at least one run, and the same figure's point estimate
  is not slower in the other.
- **No harm (required):** as in `2026-11-05-deferred-flag-walk.md`. A wall row flagged slower
  is settled by one more run on the same head, with at most three runs.
- **No retries to pass:** if no run shows a gain beyond noise, the PR is closed and this entry
  records the negative result.

# The room walk with deferred flag checks: registration and instruction count

Registered before any timing of this branch. The decision rule below may be amended only in a
commit made before the first bench comment on this PR, and each amendment says what changed and
why.

## The change

The room walk's busy phase (every lane walking, the queue not yet empty) steps all 32 lanes at
each offset without testing their flags. It ORs the entries it read and tests the OR once. If
no lane read a segment's start, the result is exactly the scalar offset's. If one did, the
offset is done again by the scalar offset, unchanged from master, from the rows as they were
before it. That path hands segments over in lane order, so the hand-over order is master's.

- **Rows in two slots.** An offset reads one slot and writes the other, so the rows from before
  it survive it with no copy. A replay steps the rows in place, and the next offset reads that
  same slot.
- **Speculative bytes.** Each goes at base + off, inside its own lane's room, so it's in
  bounds. Each is then either written again by the replay, or left past its segment's length,
  which `set_len` never exposes.
- **Speculative rows.** A start's entry gives a row with its flag in bit 23 (bit 31 shifted). It
  goes only into the written slot, which a replay discards, so it is never read. A
  speculative prefetch uses `wrapping_add` and doesn't fault.
- **Machine code.** `spec_offset` is out of line: inlined, the table pointer was reloaded from
  the stack twice per step (+0.92M Ir on a full block). The 32 lanes are unrolled, with no loop
  control. A step is 8 instructions (row load, entry load, OR, base load, byte store, shift,
  row store, prefetch), against master's 9 plus a 4-instruction turn per 8 lanes
  (`spec_offset-P0.asm`, `room_segments-master.asm`).

**Why one offset, not eight.** The Optimiser's B speculates 8 rounds per tile (review
`d143d8fe`, §3). Past a start, the speculative row has bit 23 set and can be beyond the table,
so every speculative round after the first would need a mask before its load. That is one
instruction a step, the instruction this saves, plus a replay probability of about
1 − e^(−256/1758) ≈ 13.6% a tile instead of about 1.8% an offset. T = 1 needs neither the mask
nor a snapshot.

Production is otherwise unchanged: the build, segmentation, the prefetch, the tail, assembly and
P87's in-place output.

## Measured: whole-decoder instructions

Inclusive Ir of the driver's `measured` (one `decode_block` on a fresh `Scratch`), from
Callgrind. Both arms are built from `driver/` with only the `mibz2` path differing: rustc 1.97.0,
fat LTO, `codegen-units = 1`. The input is `wikidata-independent.bz2`, sha256
`7f5c9a0044e5a305…`. The profiles, stdout (length and CRC) and consoles are in `cg/`.

| block | master 4d4709de | this branch | change | walk, master → branch | output |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|
| 0 (54 B) | 7,289 | 7,289 | 0 | short path | identical |
| 1 (899,971 B) | 20,184,311 | 19,673,153 | −511,158 (−2.53%) | 9,859,793 → 9,348,635 | identical |
| 41 (900,000 B) | 19,480,138 | 18,971,641 | −508,497 (−2.61%) | 9,676,664 → 9,168,167 | identical |
| 97 (56 B) | 7,665 | 7,665 | 0 | short path | identical |
| 233 (899,978 B) | 19,989,050 | 19,477,424 | −511,626 (−2.56%) | 9,831,055 → 9,319,429 | identical |
| 400 (899,993 B) | 19,490,067 | 18,981,100 | −508,967 (−2.61%) | 9,735,075 → 9,226,108 | identical |
| 472 (70 B) | 8,503 | 8,503 | 0 | short path | identical |

**Block 1's accounting:**
- 26,313 busy-phase offsets: 25,835 kept and 478 replayed (1.82%).
- `spec_offset` is 6.95M Ir over the 26,313 calls, 264 per offset (8.25 per step).
- The replays add about 478 × 32 scalar steps.
- The tail (58k steps at about 18 Ir each) and the build are unchanged.

A block's saving is in the walk alone and recurs every full block: this is not a first-growth
effect.

## The decision rule

- **Correctness (required):**
  - CI green, Miri included;
  - the same bytes on every corpus in every bench run;
  - the room walk's tests pass, including `room_walk_deferred_handovers`, which now requires an
    offset kept and an offset replayed, at 32 lanes and at 5.
- **Instructions (required):** `decode_block` at or below master's on every full block. Met
  above.
- **Benefit (required):** on `wikidata` at 1 or 4 threads, the CPU change or the wall change
  excludes zero on the faster side in at least one run, and the same figure's point estimate is
  not slower in the other run.
- **No harm (required), each run read on its own:**
  - a wall row (any corpus × thread count) flagged **slower** is a harm signal;
  - one more run on the same head settles it: flagged again, it is a harm, and the rule fails;
  - not flagged again, the row is reported as unresolved, with all three runs;
  - at most three runs in all.
- **Power:** control rows' 95% intervals in recent runs are ±1–5%. A harm smaller than a row's
  half-width can't be excluded by these runs, and this PR doesn't claim to exclude it.
- **Falsified, and closed with a write-up, if** the benefit condition fails or a harm is
  confirmed.

A pass establishes an end-to-end gain from fewer walk instructions. It doesn't establish that
the gain comes from instruction count rather than from the branch-free offset's effect on
overlap. Both change together here.

## Result: closed unmerged (#168); carried into #171

Two runs, bench 3.2.0, head eb3e857 against 4d4709d (archived in
`2026-11-05-walk-round.md`'s directory):

| run | runner | `wikidata` wall, 1 / 2 / 4 threads | CPU at 4 threads | walk stage (1 thread) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | EPYC 7763 | +0.3% / +1.3% / +1.0% | **+1.7%** (+0.0, +3.3) slower | +4.0% (−0.7, +9.0) |
| 2 | EPYC 9V74 | **+1.7%** (+1.1, +2.3) slower / +1.3% / −0.5% | +0.3% | |

- **Benefit:** not met. No `wikidata` figure was faster in either run.
- **No harm:** `wikidata` wall at 1 thread was flagged slower in run 2. It was not settled by
  a third run, because the change went on into #171, which staged the bytes on top of it.
  #171 was measured against master with both changes together, and passed.
- **What it says:** 2.6% fewer instructions in the walk bought no time, and the 1-thread
  point estimates leaned slower. The local attribution in `2026-11-05-walk-round.md` gives
  staging alone the whole of #171's gain. The deferred flags add nothing detectable there.

# Stewardship of mibz2's production code and releases

This document records who looks after mibz2's production code and releases, what that role
may do without asking, and how a release is carried out and checked. It holds across research
campaigns: a campaign may fail, succeed and finish, or move on to other research, and this
role continues either way. Each campaign keeps its own rules in its own entry document.

## The decision

On 2026-11-04 the maintainer was asked whether the Coordinator's merge and release authority
should be permanent or end with the compact30 campaign. They chose:

> **Permanent steward.** I'm mibz2's standing production and release steward, and compact30 is
> the current campaign under that. A failed experiment stays out of production. A qualified
> improvement doesn't wait indefinitely after passing its gates. Other legitimate maintenance
> isn't held back because of compact30.

The steward is the Coordinator, which is the maintainer's Claude Code session. The role
extended the delegation in the compact30 research charter (§2, report 266) beyond that campaign.
compact30 ended on 2026-11-06. The agent team's standing rules are now `docs/team/RULES.md`
(row A6 is this role).

## The standing objective

The objective is a measurably faster, correct production decoder, properly released. The
steward:
- keeps a failed or unqualified experiment out of production;
- doesn't let a qualified, merged improvement sit unreleased indefinitely;
- doesn't hold other legitimate maintenance back because of a campaign.

## What the steward may do without asking

The steward may open, review and merge pull requests into `master`, and may release, under
these gates.

**Changes that touch measured code** (`src/**`, `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, the bench's inputs)
merge only when all of these hold:
- the tests and parity checks pass;
- CI is green on the head that will merge;
- the CI paired A/B bench (`.github/workflows/bench.yml`) shows an end-to-end improvement
  beyond noise, meaning its 95% interval excludes zero in the beneficial direction;
- no other figure regresses unacceptably.

**Before opening a PR that changes the default decoding kernel,** account for the whole decoder,
not only the part being optimised (RULES.md C4, S2).
- **Count the instructions** executed in `decode_block` on master and on the candidate, split
  into build, walk and the rest. Use matched toolchain, flags and input, and archive the
  profiles. Charge every induced cost: work, memory traffic, synchronisation and control.
- **An excess over master's count needs a stated mechanism,** written down first: what it
  buys (overlap, locality, less contention), its predicted effect at each thread count CI
  measures, and what falsifies it. Falsified, the PR is closed and written up.
- **CI's end-to-end bench decides the merge,** not the count alone.
- **Timing on the shared development machine** is never the evidence. A workstation run is
  evidence only under RULES.md C5.

PR #155 is why: its constructor saved 19.5% of its instructions, its walk added 31%, and CI
measured the decoder 7–19% slower.

**Docs-only and measurement-only changes** merge when CI is green and nothing measured
changed that wasn't meant to.

**A red check** is handled by `docs/team/CI-INCIDENTS.md`. It classifies the failure from its
log, re-runs only the failed job, paced to the outage, and records which checks did not run. It
does not relax the green-head rule above.

**For every merge:**
- merge only the head that CI measured;
- set `expectedHeadSha` to that head;
- a later commit that changes measured code needs a fresh bench.

## Release checkpoints

When accepted production changes have landed on `master`, the steward owns the release:
- Batch changes at sensible milestones. Don't release every research iteration.
- Never release unqualified experimental work.
- Don't leave accepted production improvements indefinitely unreleased.

The release runs through the repository's existing machinery.

1. **Deploy Release** (`.github/workflows/deploy.yml`) is dispatched by hand on `master` with
   `bump` set to patch, minor or major by semver. It runs `just release`
   (`.just/ship.just`), which:
   - bumps the Python and Rust versions together;
   - updates both lockfiles (`Cargo.lock` and `bench/alternatives/Cargo.lock`);
   - writes the crate's changelog with release-plz;
   - commits `chore(release): bump 🐍 -> vX.Y.Z`;
   - tags `py-X.Y.Z`;
   - pushes both the commit and the tag.
2. **The tag alone does not publish anything.** A tag pushed with the workflow's token starts
   no workflow. Deploy Release therefore starts `CI.yml` on the tag itself, by
   `workflow_dispatch`. Creating the tag is not the same as publishing.
3. **CI publishes:**
   - the wheels to PyPI (the `release` job, `pypi` environment);
   - the crate to crates.io through release-plz with Trusted Publishing (the `crates` job,
     `crates-io` environment).

   release-plz also tags `mibz2-vX.Y.Z` and creates the GitHub release.
4. **Verify completion.** All of these must be true before a release counts as done:
   - the CI run on `py-X.Y.Z` succeeded;
   - PyPI lists `mibz2 X.Y.Z`;
   - crates.io lists `mibz2 X.Y.Z`;
   - the GitHub release exists;
   - `CHANGELOG.md` has the version's entry.

   Record the shipped version and its release commit. If any step fails, find the cause and
   reconcile it. A partial publication must not be left unresolved.
5. **Downstream:** bump wikidata-pq's mibz2 pin in a separate PR. That PR follows wikidata-pq's
   own `CLAUDE.md` and must pass its own bench gate. A mibz2 win does not certify a downstream
   gain. A package release is not permission to publish anything to the Hugging Face Hub.

`.github/workflows/tag.yml` is an alternative, for tagging a commit that already carries the
new version. `just ship-rust-and-python` is the local recipe for the same release.

**Identity.** Deploy Release's release commit is made by the workflow's `github-actions[bot]`
identity, as for every prior release. That is the repository's release mechanism, not an
AI-attributed commit. Every other commit is the maintainer's: Louis Maddox
<louismmx@gmail.com>, with no AI attribution in commits, PR bodies, release notes or
metadata.

## What stays with the maintainer

These decisions still need the maintainer:
- relaxing a gate or an acceptance minimum;
- the bench's workload, statistical estimand, repeat policy and merge acceptance rule. Harness
  mechanics and diagnostic instrumentation that leave these unchanged are the steward's

- a run on the i9 or another workstation. The maintainer authorises it by running a recipe
  frozen before the run, and that authorises that run only (RULES.md C5);

- widening the scope beyond mibz2 and its downstream pin bump.

A campaign's rules can reserve more for the maintainer. They cannot give the steward more than
this document and `docs/team/RULES.md` do without the maintainer's own words.

## Standing prohibitions

The steward never:
- reads from, writes to or calls the Hugging Face Hub;
- adds AI attribution;
- changes the allocator;
- weakens the exact checks;
- polls, or sets up cron jobs;
- force-pushes;
- treats silence as approval;
- merges an unbenched head.

## Campaigns

Each campaign has an entry document that maps its charter, roles, protocol, state and evidence.
Read it at the start of a session, after context compaction, and before any consequential

perf(bwt): the build cuts each window into its runs, one cursor step a run

build_one_pass took any window that was not 16 equal bytes row by row. Each row
loads its byte's cursor from ftab and stores it back, so a row equal to its
predecessor waits on a store-to-load forward: a chain as long as the run. On
wikidata-independent.bz2, 9.6% of all rows are such links inside mixed windows.

A window's run heads now come from one SSE2 compare with itself shifted a byte.
A window of at most 6 runs takes one cursor step and one 16-wide write per run
(run16, #169's kernel); the entries past a run's end land in its bucket above
the new cursor and are overwritten by the step that reaches them, which the
end check still proves. Windows of more runs keep the one-row steps. Other
targets take scalar run_heads and run16.

decode_block: -2.6% to -3.6% instructions on full blocks, all in the build
(-10% to -13%), walk identical, output identical. Registration, mechanism,
falsifier and profiles in docs/journal/2026-11-09-build-window-runs*.

<details><summary>How to read it, and what it cannot show</summary>

- **The four comparisons the assessment reads,** declared in bench/report.py (`assessment`): best against best (wall), CPU per byte at the most threads, amplification at each thread count, and peak RSS at the most threads. Each moves only where its 95% interval excludes no change. With no real change, about one run in five flags one by chance: a flag that matters reproduces on a re-run.
- **A trade-off is not a failure.** Faster for more CPU or memory, or the reverse, is for the reviewer to weigh against the deployment; the report names it, and nothing here fails CI but the outputs and the accounting.
- **What it can't show:** which shared resource a rise in amplification comes from (cache, memory bandwidth, SMT, the scanner's handoffs): no hardware counters are read. CI's runners have 2 physical cores, so it cannot show a knee past 2 (the workstation's is at 4-5 workers, #39). The cores' L3 is shared with other tenants and its size unknown.
- **Run-queue wait** (threads' mean count runnable, not running; schedstat): base 1t 0.00, base 2t 0.65, base 4t 1.08, head 1t 0.00, head 2t 0.67, head 4t 1.10. A pinned 2-thread run has four threads (two workers, the scanner, the reader) on two CPUs, so some wait is its shape, not interference.
- **The per-thread split's unattributed CPU** (the process's total that no sampled thread holds, sampled every 10 ms): base 2t 8%, base 4t 8%, head 2t 9%, head 4t 7%.

</details>

|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|

### Where a decode's time goes, stage by stage: the Wikidata blocks on one thread (median c/B)

Each of 5 rounds runs each build's `examples/phases.rs` once (bench/stages.py), pinned to one CPU, the builds' order alternating: the file decoded in decode order, block by block, each stage timed as it runs with the library's own functions (each stage's fastest of 2 passes), summed over the blocks, in cycles a byte of output at the reported clock (2607 MHz). **Change** is head over base per stage, paired by round as above; with seven intervals a run, a mark on one stage alone can be chance (about one run in three). Diagnostic only: the decoder's own figures are the tables above. 10 runs, 2m08s of the run.

| stage | base → head c/B (median) | head share | change |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| scanner (headers, Huffman) | 0.91 → 0.91 | 12.6% | −0.0% (−0.5%, +0.5%) |
| MTF + RLE2 | 1.22 → 1.22 | 16.8% | +1.7% (−3.7%, +7.4%) |

<details><summary>What the model assumes</summary>

- **Linear in bytes:** the scanner's time in the dump's bz2 bytes, the workers' in its output bytes.

- **The machine is this runner,** reading the dump from page cache: no download, no disk, no other work. The output is hashed by the reading thread and discarded.
- The uncertainty is the rounds' spread, with the sample ratio's added in quadrature to the part that scales with the output; not the runner's: another CPU model gives other figures.

**Two bench runs on head `eacd588`, read against the registered rule** (`docs/journal/2026-11-09-build-window-runs.md`). The sticky bench comment above now shows run 2 only, so run 1's rows are kept here.

| | run 1: EPYC 9V74 (run 42704879531, attempt 1) | run 2: EPYC 7763 (the same run, attempt 2) |

| T-vector build stage, 1 thread | **−11.7% (−12.9, −10.4)** | **−22.5% (−22.8, −22.2)** |
| stage total, 1 thread | −2.8% (−4.3, −1.4) | −5.4% (−6.8, −4.1) |
| other stages | all within noise (walk −1.2%, MTF +0.1%, scanner −0.2%) | (see the comment above) |
| `wikidata` wall, 1 thread | **−1.7% (−2.7, −0.7)** | **−4.0% (−4.8, −3.2)** |
| `wikidata` wall, 2 threads | **−3.5% (−6.5, −0.5)** | **−4.7% (−8.2, −1.0)** |
| `wikidata` wall, 4 threads | −3.3% (−7.5, +1.0) | −0.5% (−2.7, +1.7) |
| `wikidata` CPU, 4 threads | −1.5% (−5.2, +2.3) | **−2.8% (−4.7, −0.8)** |
| `records` wall, 1 thread | **+1.9% (+1.3, +2.5) slower** | **+1.9% (+0.1, +3.7) slower** |
| `records` CPU, 4 threads | +2.2% (−0.8, +5.2) | **+3.8% (+0.8, +6.8) slower** |

- **Mechanism: supported.** The build stage gained −11.7% and −22.5%, far beyond #169's −3.1% from the same instruction saving. So the falsifier (a point estimate at or above −4%) is not met.
- **Benefit: met.** `wikidata` was faster beyond noise at 1 thread in both runs, at 2 threads in both, and in 4-thread CPU in run 2. No `wikidata` point estimate is slower.
- **Harm: one flag, and it reproduced.** `records` (ab gen's near-incompressible corpus, ratio 1.0×) is +1.9% slower at 1 thread in both runs. Its 4-thread CPU is +3.8% slower in run 2.

Those windows pay the new classification (one SSE2 compare and movemask, then the `heads == 1` test and a software popcount, since POPCNT is not in baseline x86-64) on top of the unchanged one-row steps. That is about 15 instructions a window more than the old two-`u64` equality test.
  - Whether a 2–4% cost on incompressible input is acceptable against −2% to −5% on Wikidata is a decision for the coordinator. A cheaper "more than 6 runs" test (for example, two byte-table lookups in place of the software popcount) would target it, but it would be a new head and need a new bench.
- **Miri, tests and every other check:** green.
